To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(3-aminopropyl)trietoxysilane self-assembles to form a monolayer on the surface of TiO2 nanoparticles, and the structure of the monolayer can be described in detail.
the adsorption of (3-aminopropyl)trietoxysilane on anatase titania proceeds through the formation of covalent Si−O−Ti bonds.

the preferential adsorption mode of (3-aminopropyl)trimethoxysilanes on the surface of TiO2 is through the formation of Si–O– Ti bonds, with the amino groups partially involved in strong hydrogen bonds with the surface hydroxyls of TiO2.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the fundamental aspects of APTES adsorption on the surface of TiO2 and with the photoinduced degradation pathways of this hybrid material.

the structure and degradation pathway of APTES-TiO2 hybrid interfaces, which is of great importance in several cutting-edge fields of research, such as nanomedicine, nanocarriers, photovoltaics, and sensors.
the development of hybrid nanomaterials based on TiO2 and organic molecules.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the surface chemistry of APTES is much more complex than what was previously assumed and that it is not possible to predict its reactivity and stability on TiO2 without a careful experimental investigation.
APTES is able to form a stable and robust monolayer on TiO2, but the presence of the NH2 group makes it susceptible to photodegradation.
the APTES-TiO2 interface is stable in the dark and undergoes degradation upon irradiation with light.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the APTES monomer binds to TiO2 surface via covalent Si-O-Ti bond.
the APTES-TiO2 interface has a complex structure, and its photodegradation pathways depend on the nature of the surrounding medium and the irradiation conditions.

the TiO2–APTES interface has been investigated by means of advanced experimental and theoretical tools, and the results have been discussed in terms of the potential applications of the hybrid materials.
The main takeaway from our work is that
APTES monomeric adsorption is a more likely scenario than dimerization/polymerization on TiO2, with a reduced propensity of the terminal amino groups to undergo reactions.

the chemical structure and photostability of the APTES–TiO2 interface are not affected by the presence of other species, such as water and oxygen, and can be tailored by controlling the reaction time, temperature, and pH.
APTES monomers are strongly bound to TiO2, and the resulting hybrid nanomaterials are stable against photodegradation.
